blocks.text: Hyginus, in the second book of the Astronomica, under Hydra: The raven, which was under the protection of Apollo, was sent by him, while he was sacrificing, to fetch pure water from a spring. It saw a number of fig trees with unripe fruit; waiting for them to ripen, it settled on one of those trees. And Germanicus on Aratus, in the chapter On the Hydra: The raven is said to have been placed among the stars [col. 213] because it was under the protection of Apollo, by whom it was sent to a spring, etc. When it had seen trees bearing unripe figs, it flew and settled on them until they [II, 805] became ripe, and put off bringing the water. Little different from him is the still unpublished Scholiast on Aratus, whom I have in manuscript: Τιμὴν γὰρ ἔχει ὁ κόραξ παρὰ τῷ Ἀπόλλωνι· ἑκάστῳ γὰρ τῶν Θεῶν ὄρνεόν ἐστι ἀνακείμενον. Θυσίας δὲ γενομένης τοῖς Θεοῖς, σπονδὴν πεμφθεὶς ἐνέγκαι ἀπὸ κρήνης τινος, ἰδὼν παρὰ τὴν κρήνην συκὴν ὀλύνθους ἔχουσαν, ἔμεινεν, ὡς^{b)} πεπανθῶσιν [Timēn gar echei ho korax para tō Apollōni; hekastō gar tōn Theōn orneon esti anakeimenon. Thysias de genomenēs tois Theois, spondēn pemphtheis enenkai apo krēnēs tinos, idōn para tēn krēnēn sykēn olynthous echousan, emeinen, hōs pepanthōsin]. But Aelian puts it somewhat differently, Hist. book 1, ch. 47: Ὁ Ἀπολλὼν αὐτὸν θεράποντα ὄντα ὑδρευσάμενον ἀποπέμπει· ὁ δὲ ἐντυγχάνει λήϊῳ βαθεῖ μὲν, ἔτι δὲ χλωρῷ, καὶ μένει ἕως ἂν αὖον γένηται, τῶν πυρῶν περαχναῦσαι^{c)} βουλόμενος, καὶ τοῦ προστάγματος ὠλιγώρησεν [Ho Apollōn auton theraponta onta hydreusamenon apopempei; ho de entynchanei lēïō bathei men, eti de chlōrō, kai menei heōs an auon genētai, tōn pyrōn perachnausai boulomenos, kai tou prostagmatos ōligōrēsen]. When Apollo had sent it, his servant, to fetch water, it came upon a large field of grain, still green, and waited until it had ripened, wishing to enjoy the grains of wheat, and it neglected its errand. And differently again the Scholiast on Oppian, cited by Gesner, on the first book of the Ἰξευτικά [Ixeutika]: When Coronis was giving birth to Asclepius in Tricca, Corax (a servant), ordered to fetch water, neglected the task and ἐλαγνεύετο [elagneueto] was wanton; for this reason the angry Apollo turned him into a black bird, etc. But these accounts differ in such a way that it is evident they arose from the same source. So too the old proverb about an idler in Hesychius and the Suda: Κόραξ ὑδρεύει [Korax hydreuei], The raven is fetching water. And most writers, to indicate that the raven's delay was very long, imagine that it waited until the fig had ripened; for the fig is late and ripens only with the grapes, as is clear from Cant. II, 13. and Num. XIII, 24. Hence Epictetus in Arrian, book 1, chapter 15: Ἄν μοι λέγῃς, ὅτι θέλω σῦκον, ἀποκρινοῦμαί σοι, ὅτι χρόνου δεῖ· ἄφες ἀνθήσῃ πρῶτον, εἶτα προβαλεῖ τὸν καρπὸν, εἶτα πεπανθῇ. εἶτα συκῆς μὲν καρπὸς ἄφνω, καὶ μίᾳ ὥρᾳ οὐ τελειοῦται [An moi legēs, hoti thelō sykon, apokrinoumai soi, hoti chronou dei; aphes anthēsē prōton, eita probalei ton karpon, eita pepanthē. eita sykēs men karpos aphnō, kai mia hōra ou teleioutai]. If you tell me that you want a fig, I shall answer you that it takes time. Let it first blossom, then put forth its fruit, then ripen. For the fruit of the fig tree is not brought to ripeness quickly and in a single hour. Accordingly the fig seemed suitable for denoting the raven's delay and its dawdling at the water. This very idea seems to have sprung from the story of Noah's raven, which, sent out to the waters, did not return until, etc. And perhaps to the same thing belongs what the ancients report in Servius, that ravens are forgetful, and for the most part do not return to their nests at all. For the books of the philosophers do not attribute this to the raven. But the report of Noah's raven, which forgot to return, may have been the reason why the common people ascribed to the whole raven kind what was peculiar to this one. If these conjectures are true, as at least they have some appearance of truth, then that reading by which the raven sent out of the ark is denied to have returned to Noah is very ancient.

What of the fact that it is not easy to make sense of the Hebrew words as they are read today: It went out going out, and returning, until the waters had dried up? For It went out going out is thoroughly Hebraic. But what follows, It went out returning, may [II, 806] seem rather harsh, and a contradiction in terms. And I doubt whether an animal is anywhere else said to go out returning. Nor is it clear why Noah should have allowed the raven, once it had come back into the ark, to go out of it so many times and wander about for fifty days to no purpose, especially after he had learned from the dove what he was eager to know. For he could have prevented these flights by shutting the window. As for the claim that the raven returned to the ark, not into the ark, we have already refuted it above. Therefore the Greek reading, which does not suffer from these difficulties, does not displease me. Yet I put this forward, I do not decide it, and I not unwillingly submit it to the judgement of those more expert ^{(0)}.
